{"id": "5:55/q14", "question": "How does the second alladhīna relate to those who believe?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase depends on the earlier relative clause, stands independently, or is detached for praise.", "positions": [{"id": "5:55/q14/p1", "position": "It is apposition or substitution of the earlier relative phrase.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, Bursawī and others offer badal; al-Samīn defends it against the Shaykh, invokes Sībawayh, and says a relative pronoun is not derivative in form."}, {"id": "5:55/q14/p2", "position": "It is an adjective or description of the earlier relative phrase.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj says believers are identified by complete prayer; Abū Ḥayyān calls the adjectival parse most natural; al-Samīn says prayer and almsgiving describe branches of faith."}, {"id": "5:55/q14/p3", "position": "It is accusative under an omitted verb, as a praise construction.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn calls this a cut from the dependent construction; al-Kashshāf, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī and others list the same possibility."}, {"id": "5:55/q14/p4", "position": "It begins an implicit 'they are those who establish prayer' sentence.", "reasons": "The implied subject makes the phrase a new nominative assertion or praise."}, {"id": "5:55/q14/p5", "position": "It is an explanatory apposition, ʿaṭf bayān.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says what qualifies for badal normally qualifies for bayān except specified cases."}]}
{"id": "5:55/q15", "question": "What variant wording is reported around alladhīna?", "turns_on": "Whether a conjunction is present and how far the quoted reading extends.", "positions": [{"id": "5:55/q15/p1", "position": "Ibn Masʿūd or ʿAbd Allāh adds wa before the second alladhīna.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Ālūsī record the conjunction, affecting the relation of the two believer descriptions."}, {"id": "5:55/q15/p2", "position": "A quoted recitation ends after the clause about believers establishing prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Durr records ʿAbd Allāh's recitation without the following charity and bowing words in that quotation."}]}
{"id": "5:55/q16", "question": "What happens in Abū Dharr's fuller ring report?", "turns_on": "Whether the account includes the Prophet's Moses-like prayer and the moment of revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "5:55/q16/p1", "position": "The ring story occurs without the Moses-and-Aaron prayer in other reports.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and other reports say the Prophet asked the petitioner, learned ʿAlī gave it while bowing, and recited 5:55 or 5:56; ʿAmmār adds a declaration that ʿAlī is mawla of those whose mawla the Prophet is."}, {"id": "5:55/q16/p2", "position": "A petitioner receives ʿAlī's ring; the Prophet prays for ʿAlī as minister and support like Aaron for Moses; Gabriel brings this verse.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Rāzī, Elmalılı and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī preserve the report. It invokes Moses' prayer in 20:25–32 and God's answer in 28:35; details vary between a gesture with the ring-bearing little finger and the petitioner taking it, and some versions praise ʿAlī as leader of the righteous."}]}
{"id": "5:55/q17", "question": "Why are the believers described by prayer and almsgiving?", "turns_on": "Whether the descriptions distinguish the faithful, praise paired duties, or commemorate prompt charity.", "positions": [{"id": "5:55/q17/p1", "position": "The traits identify sincere, active believers rather than hypocritical claimants.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya distinguish true faith from claims without deeds; al-Rāzī cites 9:54, 4:142, 33:19 for hypocrites' negligent prayer and miserliness; Abū Ḥayyān and Bursawī make the same contrast."}, {"id": "5:55/q17/p2", "position": "They model prompt generosity and attention to people in need even during worship.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and the Study Quran say plural wording invites imitation of ʿAlī's reported immediate help; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī also describe eagerness, while al-Biqāʿī says others should emulate the deed."}, {"id": "5:55/q17/p3", "position": "The pairing praises complementary duties toward God and people.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr calls prayer Islam's greatest pillar and zakāt the needy person's right; al-Biqāʿī says prayer connects to the Creator and giving benefits creatures; Ibn ʿĀshūr says Qurʾanic usage commonly singles out almsgiving after prayer; al-Samīn calls them excellent branches of faith."}, {"id": "5:55/q17/p4", "position": "They express a continuing habit of prayer and obedience.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the nominal clause as persistence and praise for not lagging in prayer; the contemporary Turkish explanation adds voluntary submission in giving zakāt."}]}
{"id": "5:55/q18", "question": "What is meant by establishing prayer?", "turns_on": "Whether iqāma is full ritual observance or an inward state.", "positions": [{"id": "5:55/q18/p1", "position": "Performing prayer fully, at its proper times and with all required elements.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj derives iqāma from qiwām al-amr, fulfilling an entrusted work; al-Zuhrī specifies the five daily prayers at their times; al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī include all requirements and sound belief; al-Bayḍāwī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya stress conditions."}, {"id": "5:55/q18/p2", "position": "In an inward reading it is witnessing and presence of the divine essence.", "reasons": "Qāshānī pairs this prayer with zakāt as subsistence after annihilation."}]}
{"id": "5:55/q19", "question": "What legal implications follow from giving during prayer?", "turns_on": "Whether the ring act is a valid small action and whether its timing is legally praised.", "positions": [{"id": "5:55/q19/p1", "position": "A slight action such as transferring a ring does not invalidate prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī's Ibn Khuwayzmandād and al-Kiyā, al-Nasafī and the bowing-gift readers infer this from praise of ʿAlī; al-Zamakhsharī says the ring on a little finger required no substantial movement. Ibn al-Jawzī answers an objection that absorption in prayer excludes giving by saying love's intoxication can leave one alert to the companion and others. Ibn al-Jawzī replies poetically that devotion need not prevent an alert person from noticing a companion or acting."}, {"id": "5:55/q19/p2", "position": "One may give charity to a petitioner during prayer with a zakāt intention.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and al-Ṭabrisī say zakāt intention does not conflict with prayer; al-Nasafī regards the gift as permitted. Ibn Khuwayzmandād allows the prayer may have been voluntary because giving during an obligatory prayer is disliked."}, {"id": "5:55/q19/p3", "position": "The verse does not make bowing-time charity specially meritorious.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says no known legal authority holds superiority for giving during the physical bow; an unnamed Sunni in al-Ālūsī says extraneous movement detracts from perfect prayer; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the interpretation senseless."}, {"id": "5:55/q19/p4", "position": "Belief in prayer and zakāt duties can be praised without concurrent performance.", "reasons": "Ibn Khuwayzmandād offers this reading to avoid requiring the giver to be praying at that instant."}]}
{"id": "5:55/q20", "question": "Which prayer is meant?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase specifies the obligatory prayers or prayer as a characteristic act.", "positions": [{"id": "5:55/q20/p1", "position": "The obligatory prayer, especially the five prescribed prayers.", "reasons": "Al-Zuhrī specifies their appointed times; Ibn ʿAbbās contrasts required prayer with voluntary bowing; al-Qurṭubī explicitly calls the prayer obligatory."}, {"id": "5:55/q20/p2", "position": "Ritual prayer is mentioned together with charity as a characteristic religious duty.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī notes a Qurʾanic sense of prescribed prayer; Ibn Kathīr calls it the greatest pillar of Islam."}]}
{"id": "5:55/q21", "question": "What does pairing prayer and zakāt imply for law?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "5:55/q21/p1", "position": "Their obligations belong together, so separating zakāt from prayer may justify fighting.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports Abū Bakr's inference that one may fight those who separate the two obligations."}]}
{"id": "5:55/q22", "question": "What does zakāt encompass here?", "turns_on": "Whether zakāt is restricted to the later obligatory levy or includes voluntary alms.", "positions": [{"id": "5:55/q22/p1", "position": "It includes voluntary giving, and the reported ring gift can be called zakāt.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya includes obligatory alms, voluntary charity, and good works that purify sin; al-Qurṭubī cites 30:39; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says prelegal Meccan and earlier-prophet uses (21:73, 19:55, 19:31, 87:14–15, 92:18, 41:7, 23:4) and 9:103 show a broader purifying sense."}, {"id": "5:55/q22/p2", "position": "Obligatory alms, the ordinary legal sense.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī says the term's specified meaning makes the ring gift a strained reading; al-Rāzī cites 2:43, Ali's poverty inferred from Sūrat al-Insān, and the wrongness of delayed payment as objections to treating a ring gift as this zakāt."}, {"id": "5:55/q22/p3", "position": "Inwardly zakāt is the remaining subsistence after witnessing.", "reasons": "Qāshānī interprets the pair as presence of the divine essence followed by the remnant's subsistence."}]}
{"id": "5:55/q23", "question": "How does wa-hum rākiʿūn connect grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the wāw coordinates a trait or introduces a circumstance, and if so which action and sense it modifies.", "positions": [{"id": "5:55/q23/p1", "position": "Its wāw is circumstantial and modifies the giving of zakāt: alms are given during the prayer bow.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī compares giving while smiling and says simple coordination repeats prayer; al-Zamakhsharī reports this possibility; al-Nasafī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī locate the governing verb in yuʾtūn. Ibn Kathīr objects that it would imply spe

Al-Biqāʿī notes the contrast with nonbowing communities."}, {"id": "5:55/q23/p4", "position": "The verse was revealed while the believers were in varied stages of worship.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī, the semanticists, al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī report some completed prayer and others bowed, so the clause describes their state at revelation."}, {"id": "5:55/q23/p5", "position": "The circumstance belongs to those giving zakāt but signifies humility toward recipients.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and Abū Ḥayyān separate the grammatical attachment from a literal ritual bow."}]}
{"id": "5:55/q24", "question": "What does rākiʿūn mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether bowing is a ritual posture, a name for prayer, a concurrent state, or a figure of humility.", "positions": [{"id": "5:55/q24/p1", "position": "They are humble, submissive, and lowly before God or toward recipients.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī cites poetry for figurative lowered posture; Abū Muslim includes obedience to all commands; Ibn al-Jawzī cites the poem about time elevating a poor person; al-Ālūsī cites Arabic usage, 3:43, 38:24, 77:48 and poetry. Abū Ḥayyān prefers the figurative sense."}, {"id": "5:55/q24/p2", "position": "Those who bow in ritual prayer, with the bow representing prayer more generally.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī cites 22:77; Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites 2:125 and al-Rāzī 2:43 for the honor of this major pillar; Abū Ḥayyān accepts repetition as emphasis; Ibn ʿĀshūr takes it to mean worshippers rather than the bodily instant, and al-Biqāʿī contrasts Jews and Christians who do not bow. Al-Khalīl includes any forward bend whether knees touch the ground and cites Labīd; Ibn Durayd derives the prayer term from falling on one's face, supported by an anonymous poem."}, {"id": "5:55/q24/p3", "position": "They perform voluntary prayer beyond the obligatory prayer.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās specifies voluntary prayer by night and day and says the bow is singled out for honor; Ibn ʿĀshūr says supererogatory prayer draws people nearer."}, {"id": "5:55/q24/p4", "position": "They were physically bowing at the time of revelation.", "reasons": "The semanticists say some had finished prayer and others were bowing; al-Rāzī says still others had given to a poor person. This suits a general group reading."}, {"id": "5:55/q24/p5", "position": "They give alms while in poverty or a lowly condition.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this explanatory reading and notes figurative rukūʿ can denote hardship or abasement."}, {"id": "5:55/q24/p6", "position": "Inwardly bowing means attributing one's perfections to God in humble subsistence.", "reasons": "Qāshānī opposes pride in one's own attributes."}]}
{"id": "5:55/q25", "question": "What occasion is reported for the revelation?", "turns_on": "Which historical episode explains the address, and whether the ring gift is its specific occasion.", "positions": [{"id": "5:55/q25/p1", "position": "ʿAlī gave a ring or charity to a petitioner while bowing, and the verse was revealed.", "reasons": "The accounts name a mosque petitioner and often the Prophet asking who gave the ring. Some say it was silver, al-Wāḥidī's Ibn ʿAbbās report says gold; some say voluntary prayer or noon prayer. In one account the verse came first at the Prophet's home; in most it follows the gift. Muqātil reports the Prophet praising this honor. Ḥassān's poetry celebrates the special wilāya."}, {"id": "5:55/q25/p2", "position": "The verse answered ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and other converts ostracized by Jewish communities.", "reasons": "Reports name Qurayẓa and Naḍīr, social isolation, refused conversation or marriage, and homes distant from the Companions; they accepted God, Messenger and believers as guardians. Several versions then add the ring episode. Muqātil says people then began voluntary prayers after the first obligatory prayer."}, {"id": "5:55/q25/p3", "position": "The verse endorsed ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit's break with a Jewish alliance.", "reasons": "Ibn Hishām and al-Ṭabarī name Banū Qaynuqāʿ after their conflict with the Prophet, with Ibn Ubayy supporting them; other accounts name Qurayẓa and Naḍīr. Al-Jishumī also reports Saʿd joining ʿUbādah. Ibn Kathīr attributes preceding verses to this episode."}, {"id": "5:55/q25/p4", "position": "The verse was revealed concerning Abū Bakr.", "reasons": "This is attributed variously to Ibn ʿAbbās or ʿIkrima, without an accompanying scene in these notes."}]}
{"id": "5:55/q26", "question": "How does this verse connect to the adjacent alliance passage?", "turns_on": "Whether adjacency fixes the sense as support or the verse's distinct occasion permits authority.", "positions": [{"id": "5:55/q26/p1", "position": "It continues the ban on Jewish and Christian alliances by naming the proper allies.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī, al-Ālūsī, al-Biqāʿī and Ibn ʿĀshūr link it to 5:51; Ibn ʿĀshūr says 5:54 is parenthetical and the sentence resumes 5:51, praising opposite loyalty. The Study Quran reads 5:51–57 as political boundaries."}, {"id": "5:55/q26/p2", "position": "The next verse's victory promise fits allegiance to God and His party.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and al-Thaʿlabī connect taking the named guardians to God's victorious party in 5:56; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says victory can fit authority, affection, or support and cites 58:21 and 37:171–73."}, {"id": "5:55/q26/p3", "position": "The passage discourages seeking honor from outside the faithful community.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says seek God's guardianship for honor and independence; the Study Quran frames 5:51–57 as community boundaries and notes Islamic law allows treaties with Jewish and Christian political entities."}, {"id": "5:55/q26/p4", "position": "The verse has its own occasion and need not share the surrounding passage's support theme.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī argues sūra verses came at different times, notes the shift from criticizing hypocrites to directly addressing forbidden groups, and says 5:51 concerns social assimilation rather than a mere pact; adjacent placement does not prove a common occasion."}]}
{"id": "5:55/q27", "question": "How is the verse read inwardly?", "turns_on": "How ritual and alliance language is transposed into spiritual states.", "positions": [{"id": "5:55/q27/p1", "position": "Guardianship is divine care, and spiritual allegiance requires opposition to the lower self and loyalty to believers.", "reasons": "Al-Tustarī defines God's guardianship as His choice of those in His care; Bursawī's cited Taʾwīlāt says loyalty to God opposes all besides Him (26:77), loyalty to the Messenger resists desire and loves him above self, family and wealth, and loyalty to believers means fraternity (49:10)."}, {"id": "5:55/q27/p2", "position": "Prayer is witnessing, zakāt subsistence, and bowing the attribution of all perfections to God.", "reasons": "Qāshānī interprets the sequence through divine presence, the remnant's subsistence, humility and the Commander's profession of unity after annihilation."}, {"id": "5:55/q27/p3", "position": "A prefatory Persian couplet counsels accepting what has been given and setting aside a frown.", "reasons": "Bursawī says neither party had been granted choice; the couplet frames his reflection on divine care."}]}
{"id": "5:55/q28", "question": "What does Abū Rāfiʿ report around the revelation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "5:55/q28/p1", "position": "He protected the sleeping Prophet from a snake; the Prophet awoke reciting this verse and praised ʿAlī.", "reasons": "One version predicts fighting ʿAlī's opponents as jihad and instructs resistance by hand, tongue or heart; Abū Rāfiʿ later sold his property and followed ʿAlī to Basra, Ṣiffīn and Nahrawān."}]}
{"id": "5:56/q01", "question": "What does taking God, His Messenger, and believers as allies entail?", "turns_on": "Whether wilaya denotes patronage and authority, religious support, or the concrete acts of obedience and solidarity, and how 5:55 is read.", "positions": [{"id": "5:56/q01/p1", "position": "It entails obeying God and supporting or following the Messenger and believers.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, and al-Tabrisi distinguish obedience to God from support of the Messenger and believers; al-Tabrisi adds following the Messenger's command. Al-Qurtubi reports this formulation. Al-Tabataba'i argues that support is given to God's religion, which the Messenger himself upholds; he cites 61:14, 47:7, 3:81, 22:40, 40:51, and 30:47, and says the Qur'an does not call the Prophet a supporter of believers."}, {"id": "5:56/q01/p2", "position": "It is taking them as patrons, guardians, or protectors and joining their side.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i glosses tawalla as taking a wali and says the single singular wali governing God, Messenger, and believers implies one sense of wilaya; he adds that the promised victory fits authority, love, and support, citing 58:21 and 37:171–73. Al-Zamakhshari says their patron has joined an unconquerable party. Al-Biqa'i stresses seeking alliance with the source of all might. The Study Quran relates this to 5:51 and 5:55."}, {"id": "5:56/q01/p3", "position": "It is entrusting one's affairs to God, obeying the Messenger, and allying with Muslims.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi gives the three relationships separately."}, {"id": "5:56/q01/p4", "position": "In a contextual reading, wilaya here means support limited

 to God, the Messenger, and true believers.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i reports that some exegetes link this sense to 3:68, 33:6, 8:72, and 9:71. He argues against making these verses part of the prior passage's support theme, because their content and occasions differ; the Prophet cannot be made a mere supporter of believers."}, {"id": "5:56/q01/p5", "position": "On an alternative reading of the preceding bowing phrase, the allies are faithful worshippers who submit in obedience or give alms despite poverty.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i presents the consequences of reading bowing in 5:55 in this broader way."}]}
{"id": "5:56/q02", "question": "How can alliance with God be attained inwardly?", "turns_on": "The notes offer different spiritual applications of alliance rather than an explicit dispute.", "positions": [{"id": "5:56/q02/p1", "position": "True repentance is the alliance with God and His Messenger described here.", "reasons": "Sahl places this alliance among repentance's stations and states."}, {"id": "5:56/q02/p2", "position": "Alliance with God passes through alliance with the Messenger and exemplary elders, who must be honored.", "reasons": "Al-Qasim gives the sequence; al-Sulami adduces two Prophetic sayings equating honor or reverence for an aged Muslim with reverence for God or His majesty."}]}
{"id": "5:56/q03", "question": "What event is reported as the occasion for this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse's reported occasion is ʿUbādah's broken Jewish pact or the ring gift, and whether the latter report includes a succession declaration.", "positions": [{"id": "5:56/q03/p1", "position": "It followed ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit's renunciation of Banū Qaynuqāʿ and allegiance to God, the Messenger, and believers.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq connects 5:55–56 with ʿUbādah's disavowal of their pact; the report through ʿUbādah's son specifies the tribe's war with Muhammad. Ibn Kathir says the preceding verses concerned the same act."}, {"id": "5:56/q03/p2", "position": "It followed ʿAlī's giving a ring to a petitioner while bowing, after ostracized converts complained to the Prophet.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Salām reports name ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and other converts and say the petitioner identified ʿAlī; some have the Prophet recite 5:56, others both verses or the passage ending there. The noon caller's question establishes the act in al-Durr's account. Ḥassān's poem praises Abū Ḥasan's bowing gift and says God established allegiance for him. Al-Tabataba'i says Sunni and Shia reports are numerous, their wording varies, major tafsir and hadith authorities accepted them, and rejecting so many occasions would imperil reports of other verses."}, {"id": "5:56/q03/p3", "position": "In a fuller ring report, the Prophet declared ʿAlī his successor in wilaya, those present assented, and then 5:56 was revealed.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i quotes the report's continuation: the Prophet questioned the petitioner about the ring before making the declaration."}]}
{"id": "5:56/q04", "question": "Who are the believers named as allies?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase points to ʿAlī particularly, the first Muslim communities, or believers generally, and whether it resumes the description in 5:55.", "positions": [{"id": "5:56/q04/p1", "position": "They are ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib in the immediate reference.", "reasons": "Muqātil identifies ʿAlī directly and then extends the party beyond him. The ring reports identify him as the believer who gave while bowing."}, {"id": "5:56/q04/p2", "position": "They are the Emigrants, the Helpers, and later believers.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās gives this wider identification in al-Wāḥidī."}, {"id": "5:56/q04/p3", "position": "They are the Emigrants and the Helpers.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī transmits this identification from Ibn ʿAbbās."}, {"id": "5:56/q04/p4", "position": "They are the believing community, who protect one another.", "reasons": "Abū Jaʿfar speaks of mutual protection; al-Tabataba'i says the definite phrase points back to the believers described in 5:55. Al-Biqāʿī says repeating the allies states the referents and brings blessing, while describing the Messenger as formed by the Qur'an. Al-Ālūsī says repeating believers rather than a pronoun preserves God's primacy in guardianship."}]}
{"id": "5:56/q05", "question": "Why repeat the believers instead of using a pronoun?", "turns_on": "The sources give two rhetorical functions for repeating the noun.", "positions": [{"id": "5:56/q05/p1", "position": "The repetition clarifies the intended allies and invokes blessing.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī adds that the Messenger is characterized by the Qur'an."}, {"id": "5:56/q05/p2", "position": "The repetition maintains God's primary place in guardianship.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī ties it to the preceding declaration of guardianship."}]}
{"id": "5:56/q06", "question": "How is the conditional construction parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the fa clause itself answers the condition or explains an omitted answer, and whether a conditional subject needs a resumptive pronoun.", "positions": [{"id": "5:56/q06/p1", "position": "The following fa clause is the conditional answer, explicitly stating the result.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī says its meaning returns to man and fa introduces the response; al-Ṭabrisī makes man nominative, its verb's pronoun jussive, and the fa clause jussive in position. Al-Samīn notes this analysis allows no overt resumptive pronoun; al-Akhfash accepts repetition of the subject's meaning, with an understood pronoun. Abū Ḥayyān also permits an explicit noun in place of the pronoun."}, {"id": "5:56/q06/p2", "position": "The conditional answer is omitted; the following clause supplies evidence for it.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās supplies 'is in God's party'; Abū Ḥayyān supplies joining that party and prevailing; al-Samīn supplies being joined to or helped by it and says the explanatory clause then has no syntactic position. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī describes an unstated major premise: taking them as wali yields victory because it joins God's party."}, {"id": "5:56/q06/p3", "position": "Man is the subject and the following clause its predicate, implying that whoever allies with God is victorious.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī gives this analysis; al-Samīn also identifies man as a nominative conditional subject."}]}

{"id": "5:56/q08", "question": "What does ḥizb mean in this wording?", "turns_on": "Whether the lexical emphasis is common purpose, support, strength, or the separate usage of a recitation portion.", "positions": [{"id": "5:56/q08/p1", "position": "It is a group or companions gathered around a common cause, view, or pressing matter.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī reports al-Farrāʾ's 'class' and Ibn al-Aʿrābī's 'group' and calls them companions sharing a position.
